turns.doctor_question: Hello, I'm glad you could make it in today. What brings you to the clinic?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, yes, thank you for seeing me. I'm really glad I finally made it in, to be honest. I'm an accountant—well, I do a lot of auditing work specifically, and I also help run some of the mentorship events at my firm. It’s a lot to juggle, which you'd think I’d be completely used to by now, but... well, what really pushed me to finally pick up the phone and make this appointment is this issue I'm having with my work. 

I keep starting these follow-up items after my audits, or after we wrap up a mentorship event, and I sit down with every intention of finishing them right then and there. I'll pull up the files, I'll get all my notes organized, I'll even start typing things out, completely planning to just get it off my desk. But then... I don't even know what happens. I'll get a message days later from a partner or one of my mentees asking for an update, and I find out that the final email never actually got sent, or the review note wasn't uploaded to the system, or the compliance form just never got done. 

It's incredibly frustrating, and honestly, it's so embarrassing because I can clearly picture myself starting the task! I'll go look, and there's the email, just sitting half-written in my drafts folder for three days. Or the form is just sitting open on my second monitor. It makes me look so careless to my team, and I'm really not a careless person, I care a lot about my clients and the people I mentor. But it's like my ability to just follow through and hit "submit" completely evaporates right at the finish line, and it's been happening so much that I just... I couldn't keep ignoring it anymore.

symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient explicitly describes failing to finish workplace duties, such as leaving emails half-written in drafts and not completing compliance forms or review notes despite starting them.

turns.doctor_question: When you leave those tasks half-finished, what usually stops you from hitting submit—is it that you get pulled away by other things, or does it feel like the work isn't quite ready yet?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, it's definitely not that the work isn't ready. I mean, I know my stuff, the work is usually done! It's almost always that I get completely pulled away. It’s like my brain just... it just hijacks itself, honestly. 

For example, if I'm sitting there trying to review an audit file—which takes a lot of focus, obviously, because you're looking at all these tiny discrepancies and cross-referencing different accounts—I'll be right in the middle of typing out my final review notes. But then, a Slack ping will pop up in the corner of my screen. And even if it’s just a generic team channel update that absolutely doesn't need a reply, my attention just completely shifts over to it. I have to read it. 

Or, you know, it doesn't even have to be a notification on my computer. If my office door is cracked open even just an inch, and I hear two of the junior associates talking out in the hallway about, I don't know, where they're getting lunch or a client call they just had, suddenly I'm listening to their entire conversation instead of looking at the audit right in front of me. 

And the most frustrating part is that half the time, the distraction comes from inside my own head! Like, I'm currently training for a marathon—which is a whole other huge time commitment, by the way, I'm doing the Chicago one this fall and the mileage schedule is just brutal—but I'll literally just be staring at a compliance form and suddenly a thought about my long run this weekend, or whether I need to buy new hydration gels, just pops into my head out of nowhere. And that's it. That one single thought about running, or that one Slack message, or that one voice outside my door just pulls me completely off track. Next thing I know, twenty minutes have gone by, I'm looking up running shoes online, and I've completely forgotten that I left that very important email just sitting open and unsent on my other monitor.

symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient describes failing to finish workplace duties, such as leaving an important email open and unsent because they got distracted.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient explicitly details being easily distracted by extraneous stimuli (Slack pings, hallway conversations) and unrelated thoughts (marathon training) that pull them off track.

turns.doctor_question: Did you experience similar difficulties with focus and distractibility while growing up, such as during elementary or high school?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, absolutely. Yes. It’s funny you ask that, because I was actually just talking to my mother about this the other day when I was trying to figure out if I should even make this appointment. We were reminiscing—well, maybe reminiscing isn't the right word, commiserating, maybe?—about my old report cards from elementary school. My mom actually kept all of them in this big plastic tub in her basement, which is so typical of her, she saves everything. 

But anyway, we were looking back at them, and it was like reading a carbon copy of my performance reviews at the firm, just with a different vocabulary. Every single teacher, from second grade all the way through high school, wrote almost the exact same thing. They’d say I was bright, that I had so much potential, that I clearly understood the material... but. There was always a "but." 

It was always, "She loses her assignments," or "She rushes through her work and makes careless errors on small details." I mean, the rushing past small details part is exactly what I do now when I'm auditing, right? I'll just blast through a section and miss a transposed number because I'm just trying to get it done. And back then, it was constant. I'd do the homework, I swear I would do it, sitting at the kitchen table while my mom cooked dinner, but then the next day, the teacher would ask for it, and it was just... gone. My mother still jokes—well, she thinks it's a joke, I find it a little stressful, honestly—that I could ace a pop quiz without even trying, but I would completely forget the massive, month-long diorama project that was literally sitting right there in my backpack, crushing my sandwich. 

And it wasn't just the focus on the work, either. The teachers were always writing notes about how I talked out of turn, how I'd just blurt things out in the middle of a lesson because a thought popped into my head and I just had to share it right then, kind of like what happens to me now in meetings when I interrupt the partners. I just couldn't hold the thought in. And they always noted that I needed constant, and I mean constant, reminders to actually finish my work. I'd get halfway through a math worksheet, get distracted by the kid next to me sharpening his pencil, and just never go back to the math. So, yes, it's definitely been there since I was little, just... wearing different clothes, I guess.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient states she rushed through work and made careless errors on small details.
symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient mentions needing constant reminders to actually finish her work.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient reports that teachers noted she frequently lost her assignments.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient describes getting easily distracted by minor things, like a kid sharpening a pencil.
symptom_reasoning.S009: The patient describes completely forgetting about a massive project that was sitting in her backpack.
symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient recalls blurting things out in the middle of lessons when a thought popped into her head.
symptom_reasoning.S018: The patient notes that she currently interrupts partners in meetings, similar to her childhood blurting.

turns.doctor_question: Outside of when you're exercising, do you often feel an internal sense of restlessness, like you have an engine running inside you that makes it hard to sit still?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, an engine. Yes. That is... exactly it. It's so funny you use that word, because I've actually described it to my husband as feeling like a motor that's just idling way too high. And you know, people always assume because I run so much—like with the marathon training I mentioned—that I'm just burning off all my energy and I'd be exhausted, but it really doesn't work like that at all. 

When I'm at work, especially when I have to sit down for a really long, intensive file review—the ones where you're just staring at endless rows of reconciliation data for hours on end—sitting still for that actually feels physically uncomfortable. It’s not just that I'm bored with the numbers, it’s like this... this actual, physical pressure building up inside me. I'll be sitting there in my office chair, trying to force myself to just stay put and finish the section, but the pressure just gets worse and worse until I absolutely have to stand up. I just can't take it anymore. 

I'll find myself literally inventing reasons to move just to break that tension. I’ll tell myself I need to walk all the way down the hall to the main printer to grab a document, even though I don't really need a hard copy, or I'll decide right that second that I need to go refill my water bottle in the breakroom, or I'll walk over to ask a junior associate a question that I could have easily just pinged them about on Slack. It’s like I have to release that valve, you know? Because if I try to just white-knuckle it and stay in my chair, I start bouncing my leg so hard I actually shake my desk, or I'm shifting my weight constantly, crossing and uncrossing my legs, tapping my pen. It's just this constant, humming feeling, like I'm completely trapped in my own skin if I don't get up and walk around for a minute to bleed off that extra charge.

symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient reports bouncing her leg, shifting weight constantly, crossing and uncrossing legs, and tapping her pen when trying to sit still.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient describes having to stand up and inventing reasons to leave her desk (e.g., walking to the printer or breakroom) during long file reviews where she is expected to remain seated.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient explicitly confirms an internal sense of restlessness, describing it as a physical pressure building up inside that makes sitting still physically uncomfortable.
symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient describes feeling like a 'motor that's just idling way too high,' directly matching the symptom of acting as if driven by a motor.
